transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-09-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (Walden CDO), Evan Rogers (Platform Eng), Maya Li (Security Eng)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery on Private deployment options and networking model. Customer prefers minimal internet egress and wants strict key control.

00:00 Jamie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jamie from Redwood, AE, and I'm joined by Marcus our SE. Can I just confirm folks on the call?
00:10 Dr. Priya Nair: This is Priya, I'm the CDO.
00:12 Evan Rogers: Evan here, platform.
00:13 Maya Li: Maya, security.

00:20 Jamie Chen: Great. Goal today is to go through your constraints for a Private/VPC deployment, network patterns you prefer, region constraints, and any compliance items. We'll also cover what Redwood supports for KMS and private connectivity.
00:35 Marcus Alvarez: Quick note — we typically see two common patterns: cross-account VPC peering + route tables, or PrivateLink/AWS NLB with interface endpoints. Both have tradeoffs on scale and egress.
00:50 Evan Rogers: For us, the big thing is no public internet egress for inference requests. We want all traffic to stay in our VPCs and control outbound. Is that possible?
01:05 Marcus Alvarez: Yep, Redwood Private can be deployed in your VPC or peered VPC. We support private endpoints and can route ingress via interface endpoints so there's no public internet exposure. There's some setup around security groups and route tables, and optionally a NAT for controlled egress if needed.
01:20 Maya Li: When you say "deployed in our VPC" — do you mean Redwood runs inside our account, or you run a customer-managed control plane? We need to know who holds the keys and who can access logs.
01:33 Jamie Chen: Good question. We have two models: private with customer-managed control plane in their VPC or a SaaS-managed control plane with VPC peering/PrivateLink. For the strongest controls — customer-managed control plane — you retain KMS keys and audit logs stay in your account. For SaaS-managed, we offer encrypted channels and can integrate with customer KMS via external key management but there are different tradeoffs.
01:55 Dr. Priya Nair: We're processing PHI and some regulated research data. So ideally the control plane lives in our account and our KMS keys are used. Also, region choice matters — we cannot host outside eu-west-1 for some datasets.
02:12 Marcus Alvarez: Understood. We can do a customer-managed control plane in eu-west-1. We'll need IAM role setup and some cross-account roles if you want to allow Redwood to manage lifecycle operations. We document minimal IAM perms needed.
02:28 Evan Rogers: On networking, we've standardized on a few CIDR ranges per environment. Do you need specific subnets, and do you support multiple AZs?
02:40 Marcus Alvarez: Yes — we recommend at least three AZs for HA. We'll provide an architecture doc with expected subnets for inference nodes, control plane endpoints, and optional egress NATs. If you're using PrivateLink, we ask for an endpoint service connection and security group rules allowing the interface endpoints.
02:58 Maya Li: Our security team prefers PrivateLink over VPC peering because peering creates transitive routing concerns with our Transit Gateway. Also peering requires us to manage route tables across accounts. Are there any performance downsides to PrivateLink?
03:18 Marcus Alvarez: PrivateLink works well for control plane traffic and smaller request volumes. For very high throughput inference (continuous high token rates), peering or dedicated connectivity to a dedicated subnet cluster can offer lower cross-AZ latency. But we've seen PrivateLink perform adequately for many customers — it's often a tradeoff between operational simplicity and raw throughput.
03:42 Dr. Priya Nair: We're looking at ~200 concurrent inference streams, average seq lengths medium (512 tokens) and some embeddings workloads. Any rough latency expectations in eu-west-1?
03:57 Marcus Alvarez: On 3-AZ deployment with the right instance types, typical p99 latency for generation with medium seq is in the 300-700ms range depending on model size and batching. For embeddings, much lower. We'll propose instance families and quantization options in the pilot.
04:15 Evan Rogers: About egress controls — we have very strict outbound firewall rules. We can't have servers that can reach arbitrary internet addresses. If Redwood needs to pull model artifacts, how do you handle that?
04:32 Jamie Chen: For Private deployment, artifacts can be pulled from your S3 or pre-staged in your account. We can also use an internal artifact registry. For SaaS-managed pull, we can do pull through a pre-approved egress proxy or use an air-gapped sync process.
04:49 Maya Li: KMS — you mentioned external KMS. Can you be explicit: do you allow customer-managed CMKs (not imported key material)? Can we rotate keys and have Redwood not be able to decrypt without our permission?
05:03 Marcus Alvarez: Yes, for customer-managed control plane we use your CMKs and Redwood services assume a role that has decrypt permissions only as scoped in the IAM policy. We also support HSM-backed keys via supported KMS providers if that's required.
05:20 Dr. Priya Nair: Audit logs — we need to ensure access logs for inference requests are stored in our logging account and are not forwarded to Redwood's telemetry by default. Is that configurable?
05:33 Jamie Chen: Absolutely. In the customer-managed model, logs can be emitted to your CloudWatch or S3 and we don't ingest them centrally unless you opt in. For SaaS-managed, we send structured telemetry but you can disable or filter sensitive fields.
05:48 Evan Rogers: About regions — we are restricted to eu-west-1 for production, but can evaluate staging in us-east-1. Does Redwood support multi-region private deployments?
06:02 Marcus Alvarez: Yes, we can set up cross-region deployments. For strict residency, you'd isolate production in eu-west-1 only and use replication or dedicated endpoints in staging region for dev. We can also offer a fallback to a smaller model hosted in another region in case of capacity issues, but that gets into compliance questions.
06:23 Dr. Priya Nair: Okay, capacity — what's the provisioning model? Will we get reserved nodes or autoscaling?
06:34 Marcus Alvarez: For Private we offer reserved capacity (dedicated pools you control) and autoscaling policies. You can commit to reserved instance counts for predictable throughput or use dynamic scaling with a cold start tradeoff. For PHI loads we often recommend reserved for predictable performance and to avoid cross-tenant noise.
06:54 Evan Rogers: What's the onboarding time? We have a Q4 deadline and want pilot by mid-October.
07:03 Jamie Chen: We can typically onboard a pilot in 2-4 weeks if we have network info and an approved AWS account. For a full production private deployment it's more like 6-10 weeks depending on security review and IAM/KMS provisioning.
07:18 Maya Li: Do you support SAML SSO and RBAC for the control plane? We need enterprise SSO and fine-grained roles.
07:28 Marcus Alvarez: Yes, Redwood supports SAML/SSO and RBAC. In the customer-managed control plane you can integrate with your IdP. We also support SCIM for user provisioning.
notes: Customer strongly prefers customer-managed control plane in eu-west-1 due to PHI/data residency
PrivateLink preferred by security but peering recommended for highest throughput
